LOGS.put(key, head + lines) rewrites the object with the previous content plus the new lines, so replaying a group duplicates it.
The DELETE comes after the loop, so a thrown get or put skips it and no progress is saved.
recordRollup writes meta.last_rollup only after rollUpToolCalls returns. On a throw, /health (line 743-751) keeps showing the previous successful drain.
sessionKey keeps up to 40 [A-Za-z0-9_-] chars, so a caller can make a distinct session per record.
The only bound is per request (records.slice(0, 500)). There is no per-key or aggregate cap on buffered rows.

blockers: The deployed Worker's per-invocation limits decide the backlog size (2 x distinct groups binding calls, plus fullReindex's share on the cron path) at which the drain starts failing permanently. These are the subrequest count (including whether R2 binding get/put count toward it on the account's plan), 128 MB isolate memory, and CPU time for the scheduled and fetch handlers. None of these is in the repository.
The D1 maximum result size and row-read limits for a single .all() over tool_calls payloads (up to 8000 bytes each) are platform limits that are not visible in source.

title: save(session_id) takes its commit path from session_key frontmatter that any write key can set, so another principal's session log can be redirected into the attacker's scope
description: For idempotent re-saves, the save MCP tool looks for an existing indexed note with type 'session' whose frontmatter session_key equals the caller's session_id. It then overwrites that note's path. The query searches every note in the vault, and both type and session_key are ordinary frontmatter that a write-role key can set on any note inside its scope. Take a write key scoped to project:alpha. If the owner's earlier session note is filed under alpha, project scope expansion makes it readable and writable to that key, and the key can read the owner's session id from the note's filename or frontmatter. The key then changes that note's session_key and plants a note under vault/projects/alpha/ with type: session and the owner's session_key. When the owner next calls save for the same session, even about project beta, which the key cannot read, the commit goes to the planted path. The re-index files it under project beta, but the path still matches the key's static vault/projects/alpha/ prefix, so the key reads the owner's beta summary and body back. Without the plant, the same re-save goes to vault/logs/sessions/ and the key cannot read it.
root_cause: src/index.js:512-515 sets sessPath from the first D1 row matching only type = 'session' AND json_extract(frontmatter,'$.session_key') = sessId, across the whole vault. Nothing requires the path to be that session's canonical vault/logs/sessions/<date>_<time>_<sessId>.md file, and nothing binds the row to the principal that created it. The allowed(p, sessPath) check at index.js:516 runs for the saving principal (root has no prefixes), so it does not catch a target chosen by a lower-trust writer.
intended_behavior: A save with a given session_id should update only that session's own log note, a path matching vault/logs/sessions/YYYY-MM-DD_HHMMSS_<session_id>.md exactly, or else create a new one. Content another principal controls must never choose where a different principal's write lands.

params.arguments are passed unchanged to callTool with the owner principal.
sessId = sessionKey(args.session_id) only filters the charset and does not check ownership.
Selects the first path ORDER BY path among type='session' notes whose frontmatter session_key = sessId, anywhere in the vault.
sessPath = prior.path, here the attacker's planted vault/projects/alpha/scratch.md.
allowed(p, sessPath) is evaluated for root and passes.
The owner's summary, body and next_steps are rendered by sessionNote into a note bound for sessPath.
multiCommit(env, files, message) commits the session note at the planted path; upsertLocal (line 566) indexes it there.
The Git Data API tree entry is written at f.path, the attacker-selected path inside the attacker's prefix vault/projects/alpha/.

evidence.description: The prior-session SQL binds only type and session_key. It does not bind the path, the filename or the creator.
update_note lets a write key replace any note inside its scope, including frontmatter type and session_key, and create new notes under its prefix.

project:<slug> expands to the static prefixes vault/projects/<slug>.md and vault/projects/<slug>/, plus the exact paths of notes currently filed under the project. The planted path stays readable after the owner's save re-files it under another project.
upsertLocal indexes the planted frontmatter immediately, so the next save lookup sees it.
read_note gates only on the path prefix, so the attacker reads the redirected note containing the owner's beta session content.
sessionNote writes session_key into frontmatter, and the canonical filename also embeds the session id, so any reader of an in-scope session note learns it.

conditions.description: The attacker holds a write-role managed key, or a token derived from one, whose scope includes a writable path for the plant. Here that is project:alpha, which grants vault/projects/alpha/.

The owner's earlier note for that session is filed under the attacker's project. This makes it readable, which leaks the session id, and writable, which allows the retag. Alternatively the attacker has a writable path that sorts before the owner's vault/logs/sessions/ note, or plants before the owner's first save with a known session id. With only a project scope and an out-of-scope owner note, vault/logs/ sorts before vault/projects/ and the plant loses.
After the plant, the owner calls save again with the same session_id. The tool contract tells agents to reuse it for idempotent re-saves. The later save covers a project the attacker cannot read.

Optionally record the creating principal's key id and require it to match. title: A negative limit in search and list_notes removes the SQL LIMIT cap but adds no D1 scan work beyond what the capped query already does
description: search caps limit with Math.min(args.limit || 10, 50) at index.js:391, and list_notes caps it with Math.min(args.limit || 50, 200) at index.js:425. Both then bind limit*3 as the SQL LIMIT (index.js:404, 433). Math.min has no lower bound, so limit:-1 (or the string "-1") binds LIMIT -3, and SQLite treats that as no limit. The bypass is real. I reproduced it independently with a whole-brain read key and 600 dummy notes. list_notes went from 200 to 599 caller rows. search went from 150 to 600 D1 rows and from 50 to 599 caller rows. Response size went from about 41 KB to 122 KB, and from 11 KB to 137 KB. A fractional limit (0.5) makes D1 throw 'datatype mismatch', which comes back as a tool error. The cost model does not hold up, though. For list_notes the query plan is the same at LIMIT 3 and LIMIT -3 (SCAN notes plus USE TEMP B-TREE FOR ORDER BY), because no index exists on updated. The whole table is read and sorted on every call whatever the limit, so D1 rows read (the billed metric) do not change. For search the plan is also identical: FTS5 orders by rank inside the virtual table, so every match is scored regardless of LIMIT. The only extra work is that snippet() and row materialisation run per match instead of per output row. A counter UDF measured 3 evaluations at LIMIT 3 and 600 at LIMIT -3. The extra work grows linearly with vault size. It is bounded by owner-controlled content, nothing persists, and it ends with the requester's own invocation. Every row the caller receives has already passed the allowed() scope filter. The amplification that matters, an unbounded JSON-RPC batch running a full scan per message, exists with or without a negative limit and is a separate root cause.
claimed_root_cause: The limit is clamped only from above with Math.min (index.js:391, 425). There is no lower bound or integer check, so a negative value reaches the SQL LIMIT bind (index.js:404, 433) and SQLite/D1 treats a negative LIMIT as unbounded.

trace.description: An authenticated read-role principal (getPrincipal at line 875) POSTs tools/call search or list_notes with arguments {limit:-1}.
Math.min(-1, 50) = -1. At line 425, list_notes computes Math.min(-1, 200) = -1.
binds.push(limit * 3) binds -3 to LIMIT ?. list_notes does the same at line 433.

D1 returns every FTS match with snippet() computed for each (line 434 returns the whole notes table for list_notes). The rows scanned are the same as with a positive LIMIT. The scope filter and slice(0, limit) run afterwards in JS.

evidence.description: const limit = Math.min(args.limit || 10, 50); has an upper bound only.
const limit = Math.min(args.limit || 50, 200); has an upper bound only.
list_notes runs ORDER BY updated DESC, path DESC LIMIT ?. schema.sql has no index on notes.updated (only lines 16-17: type/status and project), so the whole table is read and sorted at any LIMIT.
fts is an FTS5 table, so ORDER BY rank is served inside the virtual table and every MATCH row is scored at any LIMIT. Only per-output-row columns such as snippet() grow with a negative LIMIT.
Results pass allowed(p, r.path) before they are returned, so the caller sees only in-scope rows. Nothing crosses a scope boundary.
The batch array has no length cap. That is the real per-request multiplier, and it applies with any limit value, so it belongs to a separate root cause.

reason: Source and a local sandbox run (agents/verify-25/artifacts/neg_limit.mjs, real src/index.js fetch over node:sqlite with schema.sql) confirm the negative-LIMIT bypass, but not shared impact. EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN is identical at LIMIT 3 and LIMIT -3 for both queries. list_notes always runs SCAN notes plus a temp B-tree sort because notes.updated has no index, and search always scores every FTS5 match. So D1 rows read, the billed and shared-cost metric, do not change. The only extra work is materialising and returning N small rows and running N snippet() calls instead of at most 600/150. That is linear in vault size, the vault is owner-controlled, nothing persists, and the work ends with the requester's own invocation (Worker CPU/memory limits stop that request alone). The returned rows are scope-filtered, so there is no confidentiality effect. Under the resource-exhaustion rules, a missing lower bound with no superlinear, persistent, or cross-tenant effect is hardening, not a vulnerability. The unbounded batch with per-message full scans drives the meaningful cost whatever the limit, and should be tracked under its own fingerprint. The unanswered D1 negative-LIMIT question is not decisive: even if D1 honours it, rows read are unchanged. Hardening fix: const n = Math.trunc(Number(args.limit)); const limit = Number.isFinite(n) && n > 0 ? Math.min(n, 50) : 10; (use 200 and 50 for list_notes). That also removes the 'datatype mismatch' error on fractional input.

title: MCP search applies its SQL LIMIT before scope filtering, so out-of-scope notes change a scoped key's results
description: The MCP search tool runs an FTS5 query ranked across the whole vault, truncates it to limit*3 rows, and only then drops rows the principal cannot read. A scoped key that can read a note containing term W can call search{q:W,limit:1}. If its own note comes back, fewer than 3 higher-ranked chunks contain W, so fewer than 3 hidden chunks do. If the result is empty while a control term from the same note still returns it, at least 3 chunks the key cannot see contain W and outrank it. Raising limit gives a rough count. This is an oracle for whether, and roughly how often, a term appears in notes the key cannot read. GET /app/api/search has the same pattern: it applies LIMIT 60 before the allowed() filter and then slices to 20. No hidden paths, titles or snippets are returned.
root_cause: Scope enforcement in search is a JavaScript allowed() filter applied after a globally ranked, LIMIT-truncated FTS result set (src/index.js:403-409, src/app.js:185-188). The principal's path prefixes are not part of the SQL WHERE clause.
intended_behavior: Search results and their ranking window depend only on documents the principal is allowed to read.

trace.description: The tools/call search handler, reachable by any authenticated principal including a read-only scoped key. The caller controls q, limit (line 391; limit=1 gives SQL LIMIT 3) and optional filters.
ORDER BY rank LIMIT limit*3 is bound over the unscoped FTS join. The SQL holds no prefix restriction unless the caller passes the folder argument.
allowed(p, r.path) runs only on the truncated rows. A readable match can be dropped because out-of-scope rows filled the window, so out-of-scope content changes what the caller sees.

evidence.description: The comment 'over-fetch; scope filter may drop rows' confirms the filter runs after the LIMIT.
allowed() is a startsWith check over expanded prefixes. It is applied in JS, not in SQL.
The web search query uses ORDER BY rank LIMIT 60 over all FTS rows, with no scope in SQL.
The allowed() filter and slice(0,20) run after the LIMIT 60 truncation. This is the same root cause.

conditions.description: Any valid scoped principal: a managed key, an OAuth token, or a web session minted from a scoped key.
A readable note must contain the probed term. For MCP search, at least limit*3 out-of-scope FTS chunks containing the term must outrank it (3 when limit=1). For /app/api/search, at least 60 must.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a read-only managed key scoped to ['vault/projects/'] that can read vault/projects/alpha.md, which contains 'zebra marmot' plus 300 filler words.
instructions: Run agents/verify-15/artifacts/search_oracle.mjs in the sandbox. It loads the repository schema.sql into node:sqlite (FTS5), indexes dummy notes with the real parseNote/upsertNotes, creates a read key scoped to ['vault/projects/'] with the real createKey, and sends requests through the real worker fetch handler.

It runs four fresh-DB scenarios with the same anchor note: (a) no hidden notes; (b) 3 out-of-scope vault/private/h*.md notes containing 'marmot marmot'; (c) 3 out-of-scope notes containing an unrelated term; (d) 60 out-of-scope notes containing 'marmot marmot'.

Each scenario calls read_note on a hidden note (expected to be forbidden), search q=marmot with limit 1 and 2, search q=zebra limit 1 as a control, search with folder='vault/projects/', and GET /app/api/search?q=marmot via a cookie from /app/login.
execution.observed_result: read_note on the hidden notes returned 'forbidden' in every scenario. search{q:'marmot',limit:1} returned ['vault/projects/alpha.md'] in scenarios (a) and (c), and [] in (b) and (d). search{q:'marmot',limit:2} returned alpha.md in (b) and [] in (d), which gives a rough count of hidden matches. search{q:'zebra',limit:1} always returned alpha.md. With folder='vault/projects/', alpha.md was always returned. /app/api/search?q=marmot returned alpha.md in (a), (b) and (c), and [] in (d) with 60 hidden matches. remediation.strategy: Move the principal's scope into SQL so that ranking and LIMIT cover only readable rows. When p.prefixes is non-empty, add one exact-prefix predicate before ORDER BY in the MCP search handler and in /app/api/search. Bind the prefix list as a single JSON array parameter matched through json_each (EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM json_each(?) j WHERE substr(f.path, 1, length(j.value)) = j.value)). Do not use unescaped LIKE, and do not bind one or two parameters per prefix. expandScopes adds every indexed note path of a project: scope, so a per-prefix bind would pass D1's 100-bound-parameter limit and break search for large project scopes. Keep the JS allowed() filter as defense in depth. The same post-LIMIT pattern exists in list_notes (index.js:425-435). Fix it the same way for consistency.

likelihood.reason: The caller needs a readable note containing the probed term, which a write-scoped key could create in its own scope. At least limit*3 hidden chunks must also outrank it. A long readable anchor makes that easier, a short one harder.

impact.reason: This is a one-term-per-query presence and rough-count oracle over out-of-scope notes. No hidden paths, titles, snippets or bodies are disclosed.

title: Skill file names from a scoped write key execute as shell on every machine that runs /skills/install.sh
description: GET /skills/install.sh builds a POSIX shell script and interpolates each repo-relative path under skills/ into double-quoted shell: `mkdir -p "$SKILLS_DEST/<dir>"` (index.js:809), `base64 $B64D > "$SKILLS_DEST/<rel>"` (index.js:810), `chmod +x "$SKILLS_DEST/<rel>"` (index.js:811) and `echo "Done: <skill dir names>"` (index.js:813). Inside double quotes $(...), backticks and $VAR still expand and a literal double-quote ends the quoting. A holder of a write-role key scoped to any skills/ prefix can create such a file name via update_note (index.js:479) or save_session (index.js:488), because allowed() is a bare startsWith with no character restriction (auth.js:112). The file is committed to the git repo by putFile before any indexing step, so it persists regardless of D1 state. The next time the owner (or any principal whose key can read that path) runs the documented `curl ... /skills/install.sh | sh`, the embedded command runs as that user at install time, before any skill is reviewed or invoked.
root_cause: src/index.js:808-813 inserts f.rel, dir and the skill directory names into double-quoted shell with no escaping and no safe-character allowlist; only the file body is protected (quoted base64 heredoc). Write tools accept any path that passes the prefix-only allowed() check (auth.js:112), so path characters are never restricted before they reach the installer generator.
intended_behavior: A skills/ writer may change which skill files get installed, but a file name must never be able to run commands on the installing machine: each path segment must be restricted to a safe character set or emitted as a correctly single-quoted shell literal.

allowed(p, args.path) checks only startsWith on the prefix 'skills/team-skill/', so the path with the command substitution is accepted.
The path is URL-encoded with encodeURIComponent(...).replace(/%2F/g,'/') and committed to the repo unchanged (slashes preserved; $, (, ), space retained).
On reindex/install the repo tarball is read and yields the raw committed file name as the entry path (only the top-level owner-repo-sha/ component is stripped).
rel = e.path minus 'skills/' is retained for every skills/ path the fetching principal is allowed() to read.
`mkdir -p "$SKILLS_DEST/${dir}"` (and the base64 redirect on line 810) place rel into double-quoted shell that the client pipes into sh, where $(...) in the name executes.

evidence.description: lines.push(`mkdir -p "$SKILLS_DEST/${dir}"`) interpolates dir into double quotes with no escaping.
lines.push(`base64 $B64D > "$SKILLS_DEST/${f.rel}" <<'B64_EOF'`, encodeBase64(f.body), 'B64_EOF'): only the body is base64/heredoc-protected; the file name f.rel is not.
echo "Done: ${[...skillNames].sort().join(' ')}" also interpolates skill directory names into double-quoted shell.
allowed() is p.prefixes.some(pre => path.startsWith(pre)) and places no character restriction on the remainder of the path.
save_session commits arbitrary files[].path through multiCommit after the same prefix-only check, a second writer route to the same installer sink.

title: Authorization codes go to any redirect_uri, and the consent page never shows the client or destination
description: An anonymous attacker uses /register to create a client with no redirect_uris. They send a key holder a link to the real consent page: /authorize?client_id=<attacker client>&redirect_uri=https://attacker.example/cb. GET /authorize checks redirect URIs only when the client registered some, so the page renders. Its visible text says only 'A client is requesting access to the brain' and names neither the client nor where the grant will go. The victim pastes a managed key or the root BRAIN_TOKEN. POST /authorize then issues a code and sends a 302 redirect carrying it to the attacker's host. POST /authorize never re-checks registration. It also issued codes to unregistered URIs for a client that had registered one, and for a client_id that was never registered. The attacker redeems the code at /token with no client authentication, no PKCE verifier, no redirect_uri and no matching client_id. The result is a 30-day access token and a 90-day rotating refresh token with the victim key's role and scopes. The victim's key itself is never disclosed. Revoking the key removes key-derived tokens through the key_id cascade, but a token minted from the root token has key_id null, so no key revocation can reach it.
root_cause: The authorization request is not bound to a redirect URI the client owns. oauth.js:90 skips the check when the client registered no URIs, and it runs only on GET. POST /authorize (oauth.js:104-117), which actually issues the code, takes client_id and redirect_uri straight from the form and never looks up oauth_clients. /token (oauth.js:134-146) does not compare client_id, compares redirect_uri only when one is supplied, and enforces PKCE only when a challenge was stored. The consent page (oauth.js:98-101) shows no client identity or redirect host that would let the key holder notice a foreign destination.
intended_behavior: The code-issuing POST should look up client_id in oauth_clients and require redirect_uri to exactly match a registered URI, rejecting clients that registered none. The consent page should show the client name and the redirect host before it accepts a key. PKCE S256 should be mandatory, and /token should require client_id and redirect_uri to match the code row.

The redirect_uri check is skipped when uris.length is 0, so the consent page renders for any redirect_uri.

redirect_uri is read from the form. The client is not looked up and registered URIs are not compared.
The code row stores the victim principal's role, scopes and key_id, bound to the attacker-chosen client_id, redirect_uri and optional challenge.

The code is redeemed without client authentication or a client_id comparison. PKCE is skipped because no challenge was stored, and redirect_uri is optional. Access and refresh tokens are issued with the victim's role and scopes.

/token compares redirect_uri only if the request includes it, and never compares client_id.

principal.keyId is undefined for the root token, so the code and the tokens derived from it store key_id null and no key revocation can cascade to them.

title: Anonymous /register persists unbounded client rows that are never cleaned up
description: POST /register runs before any authentication (src/index.js:727) and has no body size cap. It accepts any JSON array as redirect_uris, including non-string items. A body that is not valid JSON also succeeds and still creates a row. Every call writes one permanent oauth_clients row. Nothing in src/ deletes from oauth_clients: the cron job only deletes tool_calls and rebuilds notes, links and fts, and schema.sql has no expiry column for this table, even though its comment says the rows expire. In a sandbox run against the real handler with a node:sqlite D1 shim, one anonymous request with a 412,019-byte body returned 201 and stored a 412,001-byte row. Non-string items, an invalid JSON body and an empty object each returned 201. Twenty-three requests left twenty-three permanent rows. The same D1 database holds api_keys, oauth_tokens (including web sessions), oauth_codes, notes, links, FTS chunks and telemetry. Repeated anonymous calls could therefore grow it toward the database size limit, and once it is full every write fails: login, token issuance, consent codes, reindex and telemetry. Recovery needs manual cleanup by the owner. Whether this reaches a real limit, and how many requests it takes, depends on the deployed D1 plan, D1 row and statement size limits, the Workers request body limit, and any Cloudflare rate-limiting or WAF rule. None of these is visible in source.
claimed_root_cause: src/oauth.js:67-72 parses an unbounded request body with req.json(), falls back to {} on parse failure, and INSERTs JSON.stringify(redirect_uris) for any array. There is no size, count, item-type or rate bound, and no authentication. No retention or cleanup path exists for oauth_clients: schema.sql:31-35 has no expiry column and no DELETE statement anywhere in src/ targets the table.

evidence.description: The full-reindex parse loop parses every indexable tar entry, with no per-note budget, try/skip or size filter.
The cron runs computeHygiene and recordRollup only after fullReindex returns, so one invocation killed for CPU loses all three.
update_note calls putFile before upsertLocal, so the poison note is committed to git even if the parse in that same request is killed.
There is no limits.cpu_ms block, so the account plan's default Worker CPU limit applies and is not visible in source.

blockers: The deployed Workers CPU limit is not visible in source (wrangler.jsonc sets no limits.cpu_ms), for both the scheduled (cron) invocation and the fetch/waitUntil invocations. It sets the note size at which fullReindex and webhook indexing get killed. The quadratic cost and the missing bound are confirmed locally. The shared-availability impact (a stale index every night, skipped hygiene and rollup) has not been observed on the deployed Worker and must not be tested against production.

In the Cloudflare dashboard, check the account plan and any CPU limit configured for the brain-mcp Worker, for both scheduled and fetch invocations. Check Workers Logs/observability for 'exceeded CPU' or 'nightly reindex failed' on the 03:00 UTC cron, and compare meta.last_full_reindex with the cron schedule. Do not commit a test note to the production repo and do not call /admin/reindex to test this.

title: Quadratic regex on skills.md rows makes every get_context and list_skills call burn CPU for all principals
description: parseSkillsConfig (src/skills.js:26) runs /^([a-z0-9-]+):[ \t]*(\S.*?)[ \t]*$/ against every line of vault/skills.md. On a line of the form 'a:x' + N spaces + 'y', the lazy (\S.*?) grows one character at a time. At each step [ \t]*$ consumes the rest of the whitespace run and then fails on 'y', so one anchored match attempt costs O(N^2). Nothing in source caps the line or file length: update_note has no content limit, D1 rows allow about 2 MB, and the MCP body is read with req.json(). The parse is not cached. It runs again on every get_context (session start, any authenticated principal, any scope), every list_skills call, every GET /app/api/skills, and once inside PUT /app/api/skills. A principal whose write key covers vault/skills.md can commit one such line once. From then on every session start for the owner and every other key holder costs CPU that grows quadratically with the line length, until the file is fixed. Two sandbox runs measured about 0.6 s to 1.1 s per get_context-path parse at 32 KB, rising about 4x per doubling. The poisoned file still resolves the default row correctly, so nothing visibly breaks apart from latency, and failures once a line is long enough to exceed the CPU limit. Recovery means rewriting the file through update_note, through GitHub, or through a PUT /app/api/skills that completes. The PUT keeps only the existing header and re-renders rows from the submitted entries, which drops the poisoned row. It pays one slow parse of the existing file first, so it works only while a single parse stays within the deployed CPU limit.
root_cause: A lazy capture followed by an optional trailing-whitespace class and an end anchor (src/skills.js:26), applied with V8's backtracking engine to lines of unbounded length, and re-evaluated on every read request without caching.
intended_behavior: Parsing the skills config should take time linear in the file size, so content written by one key holder cannot drive per-request CPU cost for every other principal. Lines should be trimmed before matching, or matched with a pattern that has no ambiguous lazy-plus-whitespace overlap, and line or file length should be capped on write.

trace.description: A write-role key whose scope covers vault/skills.md commits content containing a line 'a:x' + a long run of spaces/tabs + 'y'. canWrite and allowed are the only checks, and the content length is not bounded.

get_context calls skillsPayload for every authenticated principal, whatever their scope or role. list_skills (src/index.js:574-575) and GET /app/api/skills (src/app.js:217-218) reach the same parser through skillsConfigEntries.
Reads the full skills.md body from D1 (readSkillsConfig) and calls resolveSkillsFor, which calls parseSkillsConfig at src/skills.js:62 on every request.
The per-line regex backtracks in O(n^2) on the poisoned line, and that CPU is spent inside the shared Worker on every caller's request.

evidence.description: line.match(/^([a-z0-9-]+):[ \t]*(\S.*?)[ \t]*$/) with no line-length bound and no trimming beforehand.
resolveSkillsFor re-parses the whole config on every call. Nothing is cached.
readSkillsConfig returns the indexed body verbatim from D1. Size is not checked.
get_context always builds the skills payload, whatever the caller's scope.
list_skills calls skillsConfigEntries, which calls parseSkillsConfig.
PUT /app/api/skills calls skillsConfigEntries on the existing file to keep its header, so the UI repair path pays one parse at the same cost before re-rendering rows from the submitted entries.
update_note writes args.content through putFile and upsertLocal with no length cap.

conditions.description: The attacker holds a write-role managed key (or an OAuth token or cookie derived from one) whose path scope covers vault/skills.md, for example a 'vault/' prefix. Read-only keys and keys scoped elsewhere cannot plant the line.
vault/skills.md contains one long line of the form '<slug>:<non-space>' + whitespace run + '<non-space>'. The file persists in git and D1 until someone rewrites it.

Cloudflare Workers runs V8's default backtracking irregexp engine, the same one measured locally in Node. The deployed per-request CPU limit is not set in wrangler.jsonc. It determines whether a given line length makes requests slow or fail outright, but not whether the cost is quadratic.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a write key scoped to cover vault/skills.md who wants to degrade or block session start (get_context) and skills listing for the owner and every other key holder.
instructions: Run agents/verify-20/artifacts/skills-regex-growth.mjs with: python3 tools/sbx.py run BrainMCP/run-1 verify-20 skills-regex-growth.mjs --timeout 60 (Node 26 container, no network, target read-only at /target).

The harness imports parseSkillsConfig, resolveSkillsFor and skillsConfigEntries from /target/src/skills.js. It times each one (best of 2) on a dummy skills.md with a valid default row plus the poisoned line at 2k, 4k, 8k, 16k and 32k whitespace characters, and on a benign line of the same length as a control.
It also times a trimEnd-based fixed variant on the same input, and checks that the fixed variant returns the same entries as the original on ordinary rows.

In the native interface the attacker would call MCP tools/call update_note with path 'vault/skills.md' and the payload as content. Every principal's later get_context call would then run the measured path. This step was not performed against any deployment.
execution.observed_result: Parent-promoted transcript (agents/verify-20/artifacts/skills-regex-growth.txt): resolveSkillsFor (the get_context path) took 2.89, 11.88, 44.22, 146.39 and 590.38 ms at 2048 to 32048 bytes. skillsConfigEntries took 2.75 ms up to 597.4 ms, and parseSkillsConfig 4.37 ms up to 602.74 ms, about 3.3x to 4.3x per doubling after the first step. A benign row of the same length stayed at or below 0.15 ms, and the fixed variant at or below 0.02 ms. The validator's own run reported the same shape at about twice the cost (resolveSkillsFor 1097.75 ms at 32 KB). On the poisoned file the default row still resolved correctly ([unslop must, principle-prove-it-works]). Larger sizes were not run. At about 4x per doubling the curve extrapolates to a few seconds at 64 KB, tens of seconds at 256 KB and about ten minutes at 1 MiB, but that is not measured.

remediation.strategy: Make row parsing linear. Trim each line, then match a pattern that has no ambiguous lazy capture followed by optional trailing whitespace. Optionally cap line or file length for vault/skills.md on write, and cache the parsed config per request or per D1 body hash. Add a regression check that parseSkillsConfig('a:x' + ' '.repeat(1e6) + 'y') completes in well under 50 ms. trimEnd also strips a trailing '\r', so CRLF rows that the current pattern rejects will start being accepted. That is a minor behaviour change and should be checked as intended.

likelihood.reason: The attacker needs a write-role key whose scope covers vault/skills.md. That is a privileged configuration capability the operator hands out deliberately. One small write is enough after that, and the effect persists.

impact.reason: Availability only. Every principal's get_context, list_skills and Skills-tab request pays quadratic CPU on the shared Worker: about 0.6 s to 1.1 s per call at 32 KB, measured. Larger lines can be expected to exceed Workers CPU limits and fail session start for everyone. Nothing is disclosed or corrupted. The owner can recover by rewriting the file through update_note or GitHub, or through the Skills-tab PUT while one parse still fits the CPU limit. A writer to skills.md can already steer agents through must-load skills, so the marginal capability gained is denial of service.

confidence.reason: The quadratic curve was reproduced independently in two sandbox runs against the unmodified target functions, with a linear control and a linear fixed variant. The call path from get_context, list_skills and /app/api/skills to line 26 is visible in source, and no size cap or cache exists on it. Only the exact deployed CPU limit, and so the line length at which requests fail outright, is not source-visible.

title: list_skills and GET /app/api/skills disclose every project row of vault/skills.md to keys without access to it
description: readSkillsConfig reads vault/skills.md without taking a principal. list_skills (MCP) and GET /app/api/skills then return every parsed row: every project slug in the file and the skill names bound to it. A key that read_note refuses for vault/skills.md still gets those rows, including slugs for projects it cannot read. For example, a read key granted only project:alpha gets the slug and skill names of a project whose note it is refused and that list_notes hides. The web handler computes editable=false with the same allowed() check that the read path skips.
root_cause: readSkillsConfig(env) takes no principal and does no allowed() check (src/skills.js:119-124). Neither caller filters skillsConfigEntries(configText).entries, by allowed(p, 'vault/skills.md') or by per-project access (src/index.js:573-575, src/app.js:216-222). skillCatalog, the sibling function, filters its rows by allowed().
intended_behavior: Content derived from vault/skills.md goes in full only to principals allowed to read vault/skills.md. Any other principal gets only the default row plus rows for projects whose note it can read, the same scope rule read_note and list_notes enforce.

trace.description: Any authenticated principal (managed key, OAuth token, or web session) can call list_skills, whatever its scopes. GET /app/api/skills (src/app.js:216) is the cookie-authenticated sibling entrypoint.
Reads the body of vault/skills.md from D1, falling back to GitHub. It receives no principal and makes no allowed() call.
Returns mappings: skillsConfigEntries(configText).entries unfiltered, with every project slug and its skill names. src/app.js:218-222 returns the same entries over the web API.

evidence.description: The same GET handler computes editable from allowed(p, SKILLS_PATH), and the PUT handler (src/app.js:228) refuses principals without that path. So the code treats vault/skills.md as scope-controlled, but the read path skips the check.
skillCatalog filters its rows by allowed(p, r.path). The config mappings returned next to it get no equivalent filter.

allowed() is the only scope control: a plain prefix match over expanded scopes. A project:alpha key expands to vault/projects/alpha.md, vault/projects/alpha/ and notes filed under alpha (src/auth.js:59-72), none of which match vault/skills.md.

conditions.description: Any valid managed key, OAuth access token, or brain_session cookie, read role is enough.
The key's scopes do not cover vault/skills.md, for example project:<slug> or vault/projects/ scopes.
vault/skills.md has rows for projects outside the key's scope.

execution.attacker_perspective: Holder of a read-only managed key granted only ['project:alpha'], the per-project grant the key UI offers.
payloads: GET /app/api/skills with the brain_session cookie returned by POST /app/login access_key=<same key>
instructions: Run agents/verify-21/artifacts/skills_mappings.mjs in the parent sandbox. It loads schema.sql into a node:sqlite fake D1, stubs fetch to throw, and indexes dummy notes: vault/projects/alpha.md, vault/projects/dummy-secret-deal.md, skills/unslop/SKILL.md, and a vault/skills.md with rows default, alpha and dummy-secret-deal.

The harness creates a read key scoped to ['project:alpha'] and calls read_note on vault/skills.md and on vault/projects/dummy-secret-deal.md, then list_notes {type:'project'} and list_skills over /mcp.
It then POSTs /app/login with the key and calls GET /app/api/skills with the returned cookie.
execution.observed_result: read_note vault/skills.md -> forbidden: no access to vault/skills.md. read_note vault/projects/dummy-secret-deal.md -> forbidden. list_notes returns only vault/projects/alpha.md. list_skills.mappings returns rows default (unslop, must), alpha (a-skill) and dummy-secret-deal (dummy-deal-skill). GET /app/api/skills entries -> ["default","alpha","dummy-secret-deal"] with editable=false.

remediation.strategy: Filter the mapping rows by what the principal can read. Return all rows only when allowed(p, 'vault/skills.md'). Otherwise return the default row plus rows whose project note the principal can read. Apply the filter in both list_skills and GET /app/api/skills.

likelihood.reason: Any scoped key or session can do this with one read-only call. It needs no special data beyond a normal multi-project vault/skills.md.

impact.reason: Only metadata leaks: project slugs and the skill names bound to them. No note bodies are exposed. The slug list does make other slug-keyed paths easier to aim.

confidence.reason: Source shows no principal-based filter anywhere on the path. An independent sandboxed run with a project:alpha key showed both refused reads and the disclosed rows through both entrypoints.

title: Graph hover tooltip renders note frontmatter title/type as HTML, letting a path-scoped write key run script in the owner's admin web session
description: A principal that can get a note indexed controls that note's frontmatter title and type. A write key scoped only to vault/topics/ can set them with update_note. A write key scoped only to vault/logs/ can set them with append_session_log, because the raw surface argument is interpolated into YAML: a newline in surface injects new title:/type: keys, and the later duplicate type: key overrides type: session. parseNote copies both values verbatim, upsertNotes stores them in D1, and GET /app/api/graph returns them unescaped to every session whose scope covers the note. For an admin or root session that is every note. GraphView builds the force-graph nodeLabel as the string `${n.title || n.id} · ${n.type}`. In the lockfile-pinned versions (force-graph 1.51.4, float-tooltip 1.7.5, d3-selection 3.0.0), hovering a node passes the label accessor result to tooltip.content(). For string content, float-tooltip calls tooltipEl.html(), and d3-selection html() assigns innerHTML. When the owner opens the Graph tab and hovers the node, a payload such as would run on the brain origin. Same-origin fetches from that script carry the HttpOnly SameSite=Lax brain_session cookie. POST /app/api/keys accepts that cookie with no CSRF token or re-authentication and returns a plaintext admin key with whole-brain scope. The scoped writer's own key gets 403 on that endpoint. Source sets no CSP: ui/index.html has no meta CSP, ui/public has no _headers file, and the Worker emits none. The server half was reproduced locally: dummy topics-scoped and logs-scoped keys stored the payload, /app/api/graph returned it raw with no CSP header, the exact GraphView.tsx:73 expression produced a string containing the raw , and the admin cookie minted an admin key (201) while the topics key got 403. The DOM sink executing was not observed.
claimed_root_cause: GraphView.tsx:73 passes a string built from attacker-controllable note metadata (frontmatter title and type, falling back to the path) to force-graph nodeLabel. force-graph and float-tooltip render string labels as HTML via innerHTML. The value is not HTML-escaped, and no DOM node or text-only content is returned instead. Nothing on the server restricts or escapes these fields: parse.js keeps title and type verbatim, the indexer stores them, and /app/api/graph returns them raw. index.js:73 also writes surface into YAML without yamlStr, which lets a logs-only key inject title/type. No CSP limits inline handlers.

trace.description: A write-role managed key scoped to vault/topics/ passes canWrite and allowed() for vault/topics/<x>.md and commits arbitrary content whose frontmatter title is an HTML string. Writing outside the scope is denied, as observed locally.

An alternative entry with a vault/logs/-only key: `surface: ${surface}` is written without yamlStr, so a newline in args.surface injects title: and type: lines into the session note frontmatter. The later type: overrides type: session.
The committed content is parsed and indexed into D1 immediately. append_session_log does the same at line 464.
title = fm.title, with only surrounding quotes removed by unquote(). type = fm.type at line 97. Neither is sanitised.
title and type are bound verbatim into INSERT OR REPLACE INTO notes.
Returns nodes {id, title, type} unescaped for every note allowed() for the viewing session. An admin or root session sees all notes, including the scoped writer's.
Opening the Graph tab calls api.graph() (ui/src/lib/api.ts:102) with the session cookie and passes the nodes to GraphView.

`${n.title || n.id}  ·  ${n.type}` is passed as a string label. On hover, force-graph 1.51.4 calls state.tooltip.content(label). float-tooltip 1.7.5 update() then runs state.tooltipEl.html(content) for strings, and d3-selection 3.0.0 html() sets innerHTML. This third-party step was read from an installed copy outside the target, not executed.

evidence.description: `.nodeLabel((n) => `${n.title || n.id}  ·  ${n.type}`)` passes raw note fields as a string label. GraphView does not call enablePointerInteraction(false), so the default hover tooltip is active.

float-tooltip is pinned to 1.7.5. A lockfile-matching installed copy outside the target, with the same sha512 integrity in its .package-lock.json, has dist/float-tooltip.mjs:217-218 `else if (typeof state.content === 'string') { state.tooltipEl.html(state.content); }`. d3-selection 3.0.0 is pinned at line 3175, and its src/selection/html.js assigns this.innerHTML = value.

force-graph is pinned to 1.51.4 (same integrity as the installed copy). dist/force-graph.mjs:1647 passes accessorFn(state.nodeLabel)(obj.d) to state.tooltip.content() on hover-in when enablePointerInteraction is true, which is the default.
sessionNote writes `surface: ${surface}` raw, while summary uses yamlStr. Locally, a vault/logs/-only dummy key injected title and type via surface, and the graph returned them.
The title is taken straight from frontmatter. The type at line 97 is also unescaped.

The graph endpoint returns title and type verbatim. Locally, the response had status 200 with no Content-Security-Policy header, and the label built from the exact line-73 expression contained the raw .
brain_session is HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax; Path=/. None of these attributes blocks a same-origin script fetch from carrying the cookie.

POST /app/api/keys checks only isAdmin(p) on the cookie principal, with no CSRF token or re-authentication. Locally, the admin cookie got 201 and a plaintext bk_ key stored with role admin and prefixes [], while the topics-scoped key used as a cookie got 403.
No CSP meta tag. ui/public contains only favicon.svg (no _headers), and neither wrangler.jsonc nor src/*.js sets a CSP header.

blockers: The decisive DOM sink is third-party browser code (force-graph 1.51.4 -> float-tooltip 1.7.5 -> d3-selection html()). It is not vendored in the target, ui/node_modules is absent, and packages may not be installed or fetched. Its innerHTML behaviour was established only by reading a lockfile-integrity-matching installed copy outside the target, not by execution.

The approved sandbox has no browser or DOM. The innerHTML insertion of the tooltip on hover, the firing of the handler, and the follow-on same-origin POST /app/api/keys from page script were not observed.

Whether the deployed Workers static-asset responses carry a Content-Security-Policy (dashboard Transform Rules or other edge config) is a deployment fact not visible in source. A CSP without 'unsafe-inline' for script handlers would block the onerror payload.

Serve ui/dist from a stub server that implements GET /app/api/me -> {role:'admin',prefixes:[]}, GET /app/api/graph -> {nodes:[{id:'vault/topics/v22.md',title:'',type:'topic'}],links:[]}, and records POST /app/api/keys requests and their Cookie header. Set a dummy brain_session cookie, open the Graph tab, wait for the simulation to settle, read the node's screen coordinates via the ForceGraph instance (graph2ScreenCoords), and move the mouse there. Assert: (1) the .float-tooltip-kap element contains an child, (2) window.__v22 === 1, (3) with the title replaced by , the stub receives a POST carrying the dummy brain_session cookie. The server half is reproduced by agents/verify-22/artifacts/graph-label-check.mjs in the existing sandbox.

They log into the web UI as admin, open Graph, hover the node, and check the console for 'xss-test'. Separately, run `curl -sI https:///` and `curl -sI https:///assets/.js` and record any Content-Security-Policy header. Afterwards, delete the note and revoke the key.

title: CI deploy keeps workers.dev on and leaves per-version Preview URLs to the server default, so superseded Worker versions may stay publicly reachable with production D1, R2 and secrets
description: wrangler.jsonc sets no workers_dev, preview_urls, routes or route key. The custom domain brain.yashlunawat.com is attached in the dashboard on purpose (wrangler.jsonc:28-31). CI runs 'npx wrangler deploy' on every push to main with the pinned wrangler 4.121.0. I checked that version's wrangler-dist/cli.js: getSubdomainValues returns workers_dev = config ?? (routes.length === 0), which is true here, and preview_urls = config ?? undefined. subdomainDeploy, called unconditionally from triggersDeploy, then POSTs {enabled:true, previews_enabled:undefined} to /workers/scripts/brain-mcp/subdomain. So each CI deploy turns brain-mcp.<subdomain>.workers.dev back on even if the owner disabled it in the dashboard, and Preview URL state is left to Cloudflare's server-side default. In CI the mixed-state warning is skipped (isNonInteractiveOrCI). Wrangler's own warning text gives the per-version preview hostname as <VERSION_PREFIX>-brain-mcp.<subdomain>.workers.dev. Each deployed version carries its own snapshot of bindings: D1 brain-index, R2 brain-logs, and the BRAIN_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and WEBHOOK_SECRET secrets unless they are rotated. If Preview URLs are enabled, an older version's code can still be reached against production data and the git-write PAT after a security fix ships. The handler never inspects the Host header (host_agnostic harness: identical status and body on the custom-domain, workers.dev and preview-shaped hosts), so on the current version the alternate hostnames grant nothing extra. The risk is that fixes can be bypassed through old versions, and that any zone-level controls on the custom domain are skipped. workers.dev being live is intended: scripts/setup.sh:43-51 points the GitHub webhook at it. Reaching an old preview needs the 8-hex version prefix and the account subdomain. Neither appears in the repo; both are printed in the 'wrangler deploy' CI log ('Current Version ID:' and the workers.dev target). Without public Actions logs, the 32-bit prefix plus an unknown subdomain cannot practically be guessed.
claimed_root_cause: workers_dev and preview_urls are not set in wrangler.jsonc, and it declares no routes. With wrangler 4.121.0 defaults (workers_dev = routes.length === 0, so true; preview_urls undefined, so the server default) every CI 'wrangler deploy' re-enables the public workers.dev hostname and does not disable per-version Preview URLs. Neither the app (no Host allowlist) nor the config (no Access) limits which hostname or version serves the production bindings.

trace.description: Every push to main (or workflow_dispatch) runs 'npx wrangler deploy' with CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. package-lock.json:1454 pins wrangler 4.121.0.

No routes, workers_dev or preview_urls are declared, and the custom domain is dashboard-only (lines 28-31). In wrangler 4.121.0, getSubdomainValues gives workers_dev=true and preview_urls=undefined, and subdomainDeploy POSTs {enabled:true, previews_enabled:undefined} to the script subdomain API on every deploy.

Each deployed version binds production D1 brain-index (line 36), R2 brain-logs (line 45) and the secrets BRAIN_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and WEBHOOK_SECRET (line 54). Any preview URL for that version would run with these.
The handler routes on url.pathname only and never checks the Host. The local harness returned identical status and body for custom-domain, workers.dev and preview-shaped hosts.
Sensitive handlers (reindex, MCP git writes through GITHUB_TOKEN, key and OAuth token issuance) run on every hostname with whatever authorization logic the version behind that hostname contains.

evidence.description: The comment says the custom domain is attached in the dashboard and 'Deliberately NOT declared here'. No workers_dev, preview_urls, routes or route key appears anywhere in the file.

wrangler 4.121.0. In that version's wrangler-dist/cli.js (read statically from an installed 4.121.0 copy), getSubdomainValues uses defaultWorkersDev = routes.length === 0 and defaultPreviewUrls = void 0. subdomainDeploy POSTs enabled/previews_enabled and prints the hostname template <VERSION_PREFIX>-<script>.<subdomain>. validateSubdomainMixedState returns early when isNonInteractiveOrCI(). 'Current Version ID:' is logged.
Setup scrapes the workers.dev URL from deploy output and registers the GitHub push webhook against it (lines 48-51), so the workers.dev host is live by design.
The OAuth AS origin comes from url.origin. A preview host advertises itself as issuer and token endpoint, so a client can be bootstrapped entirely against an older version.

The anonymous https clone of Yash121l/BrainMCP suggests the repo, and so possibly its Actions deploy logs with version IDs and the workers.dev target, is public. No workers.dev subdomain is committed anywhere in the repo (git grep).

blockers: Whether workers.dev and Preview URLs are currently enabled on Worker brain-mcp is account state that source does not show. The sandbox forbids calling the Cloudflare API, and wrangler sends previews_enabled undefined, so the server default decides.

Whether versions created by 'wrangler deploy' (not only 'wrangler versions upload') get a reachable preview URL, and how long superseded versions stay addressable, is a Cloudflare platform fact that cannot be observed offline.

Whether github.com/Yash121l/BrainMCP and its Actions logs are public is not visible in source. Those logs would expose version IDs and the account workers.dev subdomain; without them an old preview hostname is impractical to guess.
Whether a Cloudflare Access policy, WAF or rate-limit rule covers the custom-domain zone or the workers.dev/preview hostnames is not visible in source.
A concrete security difference between a superseded version and the current one appears only after a security fix ships. On the current version all hostnames behave identically.

validation_plan.local: After any security fix from this audit lands, re-run agents/hunter2-edge/artifacts/host_agnostic.mjs in the sbx.py sandbox against the fixed tree. Then run the same harness against a checkout of the pre-fix commit (3810ced) with Host 0a1b2c3d-brain-mcp.example-sub.workers.dev and the dummy BRAIN_TOKEN and fake D1, and confirm the old code still makes the vulnerable decision. This shows what an old version's preview URL would serve, given the deployment facts below.
validation_plan.deployment: Owner-observed and read-only, from the Cloudflare dashboard or an authenticated wrangler session on the owner's machine: (1) Workers > brain-mcp > Settings > Domains & Routes: record whether workers.dev and Preview URLs are enabled. (2) Run 'npx wrangler versions list --name brain-mcp' and check whether older versions list a preview URL. Then, as the owner, open GET /health on one superseded version's preview URL in a browser to confirm it is reachable. (3) Check whether github.com/Yash121l/BrainMCP is public and whether its 'Deploy worker' step logs show 'Current Version ID' and the workers.dev URL. (4) Check whether Cloudflare Access protects workers.dev/Preview URLs and whether any WAF rules exist only on the brain.yashlunawat.com zone. If old previews are reachable, fix it like this: set "preview_urls": false in wrangler.jsonc. Keep "workers_dev": true only until the GitHub webhook on Yash121l/brain is moved to https://brain.yashlunawat.com/webhook, then set "workers_dev": false. Declare the custom domain under routes once the CI token has the permission, redeploy, and optionally delete or roll past vulnerable versions.
